stock.counterargument: The honest counterargument is the sample: this process has not been shown to work, and a single ranking position is not evidence about one company.
invalidation: Quarterly revenue growth falling below +37.1%, the rate it was running at the quarter before.
Cash conversion dropping below 1.0×, meaning earnings stop being backed by cash.
A close below the 200-session average, which stood at $130.33 on the decision date.
risks: The share count is from 2026-06-30, 119 days older than the price, so the market capitalisation carries that staleness.
The most recent filing covers a period ending 2026-06-30, 119 days before the decision date.
One of the four quarters in the trailing year is the fourth quarter, which companies report only as part of the full year; it is derived as the annual figure less the first three quarters.
Point-in-time fundamentals are built from filings accepted up to 2026-10-27.

earnings.basis: the same fiscal quarter's announcement a year earlier (2026-02-25) plus 364 days

stock.rule: Universe: every US-listed common stock on NYSE, Nasdaq or NYSE American — about 4,700 names from Nasdaq Trader's own file. Eligible means: priced at $5 or more, median daily turnover of $20M or more over 60 sessions, at least 253 sessions of history, a 10-Q or 10-K whose period ended within 200 days, close above the 200-session average, volatility inside the day's 85th percentile, debt no more than 6× operating cash flow, no results announced in the last 2 sessions, and no position already open in the stock or a fourth in the same SIC division. Eligible candidates are then ranked on equally weighted z-scores within their sector group, over the signals that are defined for that group. One position per session, held 21 sessions, a twenty-first of capital each, 10 basis points of cost each way. Fundamentals are read as they stood on the decision date, never as they read today. The score is a ranking position among that day's eligible candidates. It is not a probability, a price target, or a forecast of any return.
stock.validation: The held-out window has not been opened. No claim of an edge is made or implied.

stories.title: MCP vs API Calls: Which Should You Use for Python LLM Apps?
stories.excerpt: MCP vs API calls: build one Python tool, integrate it both ways, and compare. Learn what each approach costs and when an MCP server pays for itself.
stories.lead:
Anthropic open-sourced the Model Context Protocol (MCP) in November 2024 to fix a scaling problem: every new tool a model reached for needed its own integration, built on direct API calls. Building that integration today involves a decision usually framed as MCP vs API calls.

One year later, more than 10,000 public MCP servers were running. ChatGPT, Gemini, Cursor, and Microsoft Copilot had all added support, and Anthropic had donated the protocol to the Linux Foundation. So it’s tempting to see direct API calls as the old way to connect a tool and MCP as what comes next.

stories.title: Exploring AI Coding Agent Workflows
stories.excerpt: AI coding agents come in four types: IDE, terminal, PR, and cloud. Learn how each workflow fits into modern Python development.
stories.lead:
AI coding agents can read your code, reason about changes, and act on your behalf. To choose the right one, it helps to understand the four common workflow types: integrated development environment (IDE), terminal, pull request (PR), and cloud.

Whether you’re pairing with an agent in your editor or handing off whole tasks to the cloud, you’ll come away knowing how much control each workflow gives you and where it’s most likely to trip you up.

stories.title: Luxury cruise passengers stranded in Cambodia due to soaring fuel costs
stories.excerpt: The Villa Vie Odyssey suspended its voyage and is working with passengers on "temporary living arrangements".
stories.lead:
A luxury cruise ship on a years-long voyage around the world said it suspended operations due to extraordinarily high fuel costs, leaving passengers stranded in Cambodia.

The US-based operator of Villa Vie Odyssey said it was working with passengers on disembarkation plans and "temporary living arrangements".

It is unclear how many were on board but the nearly 200m (656ft) vessel can carry up to 650 passengers. It departed Belfast in October 2024 for a "continuous voyage around the world".

stories.title: Netanyahu and Eisenkot face difficult paths to power as neither set to win majority
stories.excerpt: The two main blocs appear to have too few seats to form the next government without reliance on Arab parties.
stories.lead:
With results still trickling in, it currently appears that Israel's veteran Prime Minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has done better than was widely predicted with his Likud emerging as the largest single party.

His existing bloc with ultra-nationalist and ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties appear to be just short of a 61-seat majority in the 120-seat parliament. However, analysts caution that this is subject to change because the early count was skewed towards areas known to have strong right-wing support.

A dramatic deadlock had been widely forecast as Israelis surged to the polls – with turnout reaching more than 77%.

stories.title: Why many student voters have a right to choose where to register to vote
stories.excerpt: Student voters studying outside their hometown have a right to choose where they register to vote. Advocates say a Montana legal fight is a reminder of a misunderstanding of those students' rights.
stories.lead:
Many student voters studying outside their hometown face a key decision before they even get a ballot: Should they register to vote where they go to school?

A Supreme Court ruling in 1979 affirmed the right of eligible students to register in the communities where they live during the academic year. But close to a half-century later, some people continue to question why students can vote in their college towns.

City experts are welcoming reports that chancellor John Healey will scrap plans to slash the annual cash Isa allowance from £20,000 to £12,000 a year.

stories.title: Men's Water Polo Salvages Weekend vs. Saint Mary's
stories.excerpt: Carrington, Crimson dominate second quarter to pull away in early back-and-forth.
stories.lead:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- The No. 18 Harvard men's water polo team capped the Julian Fraser Memorial Tournament at Santa Clara with a 17-11 win over Saint Mary's on Sunday morning. The Crimson salvaged the weekend and improved to 11-12 overall, while the Gaels dropped to 7-12.

First-year Clay Carrington led all players with six goals plus one assist. He was held off the scoresheet in the first quarter with Harvard down 4-3 at the break. In the second, Carrington cashed in for four goals, including one late in the half to go on top 8-7 before intermission.

stories.title: Win Streak Snapped at Seven Games for Men's Water Polo
stories.excerpt: No. 18 Crimson fall in top-20 match-up with No. 13 Pacific.
stories.lead:
SANTA CLARA, Calif. -- The No. 18 Harvard men's water polo team lost to No. 13 Pacific, 12-6, in its first game at the Julian Fraser Memorial Tournament hosted by Santa Clara. The Crimson saw its seven-game win streak snapped as it dropped to 10-11 on the season.

Juniors Lukas Peabody and Dean Strauser led Harvard with two goals and one assist apiece. Senior attacker Vilas Sogaard-Srikrishnan was pressed into action in the net again and provided 10 saves.

The Crimson are back in action on Saturday at 5:20 p.m. ET against No. 10 UC Davis.
